headline: Three men plead guilty in New Hampshire bobcat-poaching scheme
dek: Federal prosecutors say at least 41 bobcats were illegally killed in New Hampshire, falsely tagged in New York and shipped to Canada for sale.
body: Three New Hampshire men pleaded guilty this week in a federal case that prosecutors say involved the illegal killing of at least 41 bobcats and the shipment of their pelts to Canada. The pleas add a major development to a long-running wildlife investigation spanning New Hampshire, New York and Canada. The [U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Hampshire](https://www.justice.gov/usao-nh/pr/three-men-plead-guilty-poaching-more-40-bobcats-and-exporting-them-canada) announced the pleas Friday.

Sherwood Dubrey Jr., 48, and Randy Inman, 49, pleaded guilty to conspiring to violate the federal Lacey Act. Sherwood Dubrey Sr., 72, pleaded guilty to a Lacey Act violation. All three appeared before U.S. District Judge Joseph N. Laplante, and the court scheduled their sentencings for January 2027. The younger Dubrey and Inman each face a maximum of five years in prison and up to three years of supervised release. The elder Dubrey faces a maximum of one year in prison and up to one year of supervised release. Those are statutory maximums, not predictions of the sentences the judge will impose.

According to the federal account, Dubrey Jr. and Inman killed bobcats in New Hampshire from 2018 through 2022, then moved the pelts to New York. Dubrey Sr. allegedly obtained false CITES tags there so the animals would appear to have been legally taken in a state with a bobcat hunting season. The pelts were then exported to Canada and offered at a fur auction. Prosecutors say the scheme involved at least 41 illegally exported pelts. [New Hampshire Public Radio](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-02/poaching-bobcats-nh-newhampshire-operation-night-cat) independently reported the same sequence and described the case as one of the state’s largest recent poaching investigations.

The case matters because New Hampshire does not allow bobcat hunting or trapping. The Justice Department says the Lacey Act, enacted in 1900, prohibits wildlife violations that cross state or international borders. A lawfully harvested bobcat pelt also requires a tag under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, or CITES. New York has a legal bobcat season and an export program, while New Hampshire has neither because taking the animals is unlawful. The alleged movement of pelts across state lines therefore was not a paperwork technicality; it was central to making illegally taken wildlife appear eligible for international trade.

Investigators say the animals were lured with bait piles placed on the men’s property and on state land before being shot. The Justice Department said text messages and photographs or videos from rifles with scopes documented the conduct, and that messages showed the defendants knew the killings were illegal. New Hampshire Fish and Game conservation officers and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service led the investigation, with assistance from agencies in New York, Canada and Massachusetts as well as the FBI. The federal release attributes those details to the public record and investigative evidence; NorthEast News has not independently reviewed the underlying files.

NHPR reported that the federal pleas are part of Operation Night Cat, a New Hampshire Fish and Game investigation that previously produced state convictions in 2024 for related hunting violations. Inman and Dubrey Jr. are former corrections officers at the New Hampshire State Prison for Men, according to NHPR. The public radio report also said the broader investigation uncovered allegations of potential crimes by prison staff that authorities reviewed but did not charge. Those separate allegations are not part of the federal bobcat pleas and should not be treated as proven conduct.

The wildlife backdrop is unusually clear in state records. New Hampshire Fish and Wildlife’s [2023-24 furbearer report](https://www.nhfishandwildlife.com/assets/Performance-reports/W89R21-Projects%205-8%20Combined%20Final%202024.pdf) says the bobcat season remained closed; trappers reported 36 incidental captures that were released and one bobcat reported killed. That dated report is not a current population estimate, but it explains why the state treats unauthorized killing as a conservation and enforcement issue rather than an unregulated harvest. Federal officials also said the case threatened the tagging system used to keep wildlife trade legal and sustainable.

The next formal step is sentencing in January. The Justice Department says the investigation involved cooperation across multiple jurisdictions, underscoring why wildlife cases can become federal matters when animals or pelts cross borders. The guilty pleas resolve the defendants’ responsibility for the charges to which they admitted, but the judge will still determine penalties. For New Hampshire, the case leaves a concrete reminder that the state’s closed bobcat season applies even when a pelt is later moved somewhere that has different hunting rules—and that false origin documents do not erase where protected wildlife was actually taken.
